passages.title: Email Correspondence: Disputing a Recurring Charge

emails.subject: Cancelled membership still being charged — member 55912
emails.body:
Dear Vantage Fitness,

I cancelled my membership on 12 March, in person at the Kingsway branch, and was told the final payment would be the one taken on 1 April. I have now been charged $64.99 on 1 April, 1 May and 1 June.

When I called on 20 May I was told there was no cancellation on file. The staff member suggested I might have spoken to someone at the desk rather than completing a form. I was not given a form and was not told one existed; I was told the cancellation was done and that I would receive an email. No email arrived, which I should have followed up on, and did not.

I have my bank statements showing the three payments, and I can describe the member of staff I spoke to. I do not have a reference number because none was offered.

I am asking for the April, May and June payments to be refunded — $194.97 — and for the membership to be closed with written confirmation this time. I would also like to know whether cancellations are recorded in any way at the branch, because if they are not, I doubt I am the only person this has happened to.

Regards,
Ingrid Solberg

emails.subject: RE: Cancelled membership still being charged — member 55912
emails.body:
Dear Ms Solberg,

I am sorry. You are right on every point that matters, and I would rather say so plainly than manage the conversation.

Our branch system does log desk enquiries, and there is an entry against your member number on 12 March recording a cancellation request. It was never escalated to a cancellation form, which is the step that actually stops the billing. The entry existed the whole time you were being told there was no record of it, and the colleague who took your call on 20 May was looking at a different screen. That is our failure twice over.

All three payments are refunded — $194.97 — processed today and typically visible in three to five business days. Your membership is closed as of 12 March, the date you originally asked, and written confirmation is attached to this email.

On your last question, and I think it is the useful one: you are not the only person. We have found eleven similar cases since January. We are changing the process so a desk cancellation generates the form automatically rather than relying on staff to complete a second step, and so the member receives the confirmation email before leaving the building. That will not help the other ten until we contact them, which we are now doing.

Regards,
Marcus Dell
Customer Resolution

passages.title: What a Credit Score Actually Measures
passages.content:
Few numbers are as widely discussed and as poorly understood as the credit score. Much of the confusion comes from treating it as a judgement of financial virtue. It is not. It is a prediction of one narrow thing: the likelihood that a borrower will fall ninety days behind on a payment within the next two years.

That definition explains most of the behaviour people find counter-intuitive. Someone who has never borrowed has no score, not a good one, because there is nothing to predict from. A person who pays off a card in full every month and a person who carries a small balance and pays the minimum may score similarly on payment history, even though their finances differ enormously. The score is not measuring wealth, income or prudence. Income is not an input at all.

Payment history is the largest single component, typically about a third of the calculation, and within it recency matters more than volume. A missed payment last month weighs far more heavily than three missed payments six years ago. This is why the standard advice to pay on time even if paying only the minimum is sound: the score cares more about whether the payment happened than about how large it was.

The second component, usually around thirty per cent, is credit utilisation — the proportion of available credit currently in use. This is the source of the most common piece of accidental self-harm. Closing an unused card reduces total available credit, which raises utilisation on the remaining cards even though nothing about the person's borrowing has changed. Cancelling a card in an attempt to appear responsible frequently lowers the score.

Length of history, the mix of credit types and recent applications make up the remainder. Applications are the one most often misjudged: a formal application creates a hard enquiry that is visible to lenders, while checking one's own score is a soft enquiry and has no effect whatever. The belief that looking at your own score damages it is entirely false, and it deters exactly the people who would benefit most from looking.

Errors are more common than most people assume. Roughly one report in five contains a material error, and correcting one is free. The bureau must investigate a disputed item, usually within thirty days, and remove anything it cannot verify.

passages.title: Should Businesses Be Required to Accept Cash?

viewpoints.name: Dolores Ferreira, corner shop owner
viewpoints.text: I went card-only for eight months and I have gone back. The processing fees were about one and a half per cent of everything I sold, which on my margins is a serious sum, and I lost customers I did not expect to lose — older regulars, and people who budget in cash precisely because it is visible and finite. What I will not accept is being told this is nostalgia. It is a payment method that costs me less and that a portion of my customers prefer. That should be my decision, not a mandate in either direction.

viewpoints.name: Arun Chatterjee, financial inclusion researcher
viewpoints.text: About one adult in twenty here has no bank account, and the figure is far higher among recent arrivals, people leaving abusive relationships, and those without fixed address. For them a cashless shop is simply a shop they cannot use. I hear the argument that they should open an account, which assumes the barrier is ignorance rather than identification requirements, minimum balances and a history of being turned away. Until those are fixed, refusing cash excludes people who have no alternative.

viewpoints.name: Wendy Lam, retail operations director
viewpoints.text: Handling cash is not free either, and this is consistently left out. We pay for secure collection, insurance, till reconciliation and the staff time to count it, and we absorb the losses from mistakes and theft. In our stores the all-in cost of cash is slightly above card. I do not want a mandate, but I would ask that the debate compare the real cost of both rather than treating cash as costless because no percentage appears on a statement.

viewpoints.name: Sgt. Marie Boucher, community policing
viewpoints.text: My interest is narrower than the others'. Businesses that go cashless see a sharp fall in robbery, and that is not a marginal effect — there is nothing on the premises worth the risk. Against that, cash is the only payment method that cannot be frozen, tracked or cut off, which matters to people fleeing a controlling partner. I am not going to pretend those two facts resolve neatly. I would only ask that whoever writes the rule has actually weighed both, rather than the one that suits their argument.
